title: Foundation for Innovations in Health: Website Rebuild | Studio 1947
description: We rebuilt fihruralhealth.org for a rural health non-profit: one clear route through the work, pages that open in under a second, photography from the field, and a design system the team can run without us.
ogTitle: Foundation for Innovations in Health: Website Rebuild | Studio 1947
ogDescription: A rural health non-profit's website, rebuilt around one question: can a donor understand this work in ninety seconds?

hero.alt: The Foundation for Innovations in Health website on desktop and mobile: the Health for a billion homepage beside the contact screen, on an olive ground

body: The Foundation for Innovations in Health runs digital clinics in Birbhum, a medical boat in the Sundarbans, and training programmes that put rural young people into hospital jobs. It is complicated work, done in places most donors will never visit.

All of that had to fit on a website, and the earlier one asked visitors to do the assembling themselves. Our brief was simple to say and hard to do. A CSR head with ninety seconds should be able to understand what FIH does, believe it is real, and know how to fund it.

sections.label: The rebuilt site
sections.heading: fihruralhealth.org
body: One sentence carries the whole organisation, and everything below it is proof. Health for a billion sits alone at the top of the page, followed immediately by the two things FIH actually does.

media.alt: FIH homepage hero: the headline Health for a billion beside an illustration of hands holding a map of India
media.caption: The homepage opens with the mission and two buttons, not a slideshow

media.alt: Two programme cards on the FIH homepage: Accessible Primary Care and Employment-Oriented Education
media.caption: The whole organisation as two doors: healthcare and education. Everything else lives behind one of them

sections.heading: Cutting it down
sections.label: Simplification
body: The hardest part of this project was not building anything. It was deciding what to leave out.

FIH does a great deal, and every part of it matters to someone inside the organisation. But a visitor is not reading a report. They are scanning, deciding whether to trust you, and leaving. So we made a rule for the whole site. One idea per screen, and no screen that exists only to introduce another screen.

cards.title: Two paths, not twelve
cards.body: Healthcare and education. Every programme, project and story hangs off one of those two, so nobody has to hold a menu in their head.

cards.title: Numbers where the claim is
cards.body: Clinic counts, cost per visit and placement figures sit next to the sentence they support, instead of collecting in a statistics page nobody opens.

cards.title: Plain words
cards.body: Task-shifting became what it actually means: a trained health worker does the visit, a doctor joins by video. The jargon stayed for the people who need it, further down.

sections.heading: The work, shown as work
sections.label: Visual ethnography
body: Non-profit websites tend to fill up with stock photography, and it costs them the one thing they cannot buy back, which is being believed. Nothing on this site is bought.

Every image is from the field. The boat clinic pulling into a bank in the Sundarbans, a health worker with a tablet, a classroom of trainees, a scan room. We treated the photography as evidence rather than decoration, so we kept the frames wide, left the ordinary details in, and wrote captions that say where you are and what is happening.
The same rule shaped Stories of Change. Real faces, real names, real jobs, laid out as a wall of portraits you can scroll through. It reads like a village, which is what it is.

sections.heading: Built to open fast
sections.label: Performance
body: A lot of this site's audience is on a phone on a rural network. A page that takes six seconds does not get read, however good it is. So speed was a design constraint from the first day, not a cleanup task at the end.

The site is a Next.js application on the App Router with Tailwind, serving pre-rendered pages, modern image formats sized to their slot, and fonts that never block the first paint. Measured from a cold load on a desktop connection, here is where it lands.

sections.heading: One kit, many pages
sections.label: Design system
body: Everything on the site is assembled from a small set of parts, so a new programme page can be built in an afternoon and still look like it belongs.

Amber is the only accent colour and it is reserved for one job, which is telling you where to act. Every donate button, every active state, every eyebrow label. Black carries structure, white carries reading. Poppins for headings, Lato for body text, both chosen for how they hold up at small sizes on a cheap screen.
list: Programme card. Image, label, title, one line, one button. Used for healthcare, education, projects and campaigns.
Spotlight band. A full-width photograph with a story panel beside it, for the boat clinic and other flagship projects.
Pull quote. A single amber screen with a field quote, used sparingly so it keeps its force.
Portrait wall. The layout behind both Stories of Change and the mentor group.
Notification bell. Live field updates from the CMS, with unread state remembered between visits.

sections.heading: Made for a phone first
sections.label: Responsive
body: The mobile layout is not the desktop one squeezed. The headline breaks to fit the width it actually has, the menu collapses to a single button, the notification bell stays reachable with a thumb, and the two programme doors stack in the order they matter.
Type sizes were set by reading the site outdoors on a mid-range Android phone, which is closer to how it gets used than any lab test.

media.alt: The FIH homepage on an iPhone, showing the collapsed navigation and stacked hero
media.caption: The homepage on a phone

sections.heading: The team runs it now
sections.label: Handover
body: The site is wired to Sanity, so field staff publish health camps, alerts and new stories themselves. Nobody has to file a ticket with a developer to announce a camp that is happening on Saturday.
That was the real deliverable. A website a non-profit needs a studio to update is a website that goes stale by the second month.

cards.title: Published by the people who were there
cards.body: Field teams post updates and photographs from their own phones, and the notification bell surfaces them across the site.

cards.title: Trust made visible
cards.body: Board members, academic partners, CSR funders and 80G status are all one click from the homepage, where partners look for them.

cards.title: Fast enough for the last mile
cards.body: Pages open in about a second on desktop and stay light on mobile data, which is where most of this audience actually is.
